lead: An SCR in forward blocking turns on when something starts its internal regeneration. Gate current is the method designers use, because it fixes the instant of turn-on; heat, excessive voltage and a fast voltage rise do it by accident, and light is used on purpose in HVDC valves. A trigger circuit must give a fast pulse with enough current, lasting until the anode current passes the latching current, within the gate's power limits. The R, RC and UJT circuits and the pulse transformer are the standard exam circuits.
prereq: You need: latching current and the two-transistor model of the SCR chapter.

sections.h3: Five ways to turn on an SCR

items: Gate triggering: a positive gate-cathode current injects carriers into P2, regeneration starts and the SCR latches. This is the normal, controlled method.
Forward-voltage triggering: raising V<sub>AK</sub> to V<sub>BO</sub> breaks down J2; it can damage the device, so it is not used for control.
dv/dt triggering: a fast rise of anode voltage drives a charging current C<sub>j</sub> dv/dt through the capacitance of J2, which acts like gate current. Snubbers prevent it.
Temperature triggering: leakage rises steeply with junction temperature until it alone starts regeneration. Good heat sinking prevents it.
Light triggering: light on the gate region creates carriers. The light-activated SCR (LASCR) is fired through optical fibre in HVDC valves, isolating the control.

sections.h3: Gate ratings and the gate pulse

blocks.text: The gate-cathode path is a p-n junction, so its V–I curve is like a diode's and it varies from one device to the next. The datasheet gives V<sub>GT</sub> and I<sub>GT</sub>, the gate voltage and current that are sure to trigger every device of that type at a stated temperature; the drive must supply at least these, with margin for cold days. It also gives maximum limits: peak gate voltage and current, and peak and average gate power P<sub>GM</sub> and P<sub>G(AV)</sub>. The operating point must lie between the ‘sure trigger’ values and these limits.

where R<sub>s</sub> is the series gate resistor (Ω), V<sub>s</sub> the trigger source voltage (V), V<sub>GT</sub> the gate trigger voltage (V) and I<sub>GT</sub> the gate trigger current (A). The resistor and the gate see the peak power only while the pulse is on; the average power is the peak power times the pulse duty ratio.

A good gate pulse rises in well under a microsecond with an initial current several times I<sub>GT</sub> (hard triggering), so the whole cathode turns on quickly. It must last until the anode current passes I<sub>L</sub>, which with an inductive load can take hundreds of microseconds. Firing circuits often send a burst of short pulses (a pulse train): it keeps a pulse transformer out of saturation, cuts gate power, and supplies a pulse whenever the SCR becomes forward-biased.

sections.h3: Trigger circuits: R, RC, UJT and pulse transformer

items: R triggering: on an AC supply, a resistor (with a diode) feeds gate current from the anode voltage itself. The SCR fires when the gate current reaches I<sub>GT</sub>, which can happen only while the supply is rising, so the firing angle can be varied from about 0° to 90° only.

RC triggering: a capacitor in the gate network charges through a variable resistor. The capacitor voltage lags the supply, so the gate threshold is reached later in the cycle; the firing angle can be varied from about 0° to nearly 180°.

UJT relaxation oscillator: a unijunction transistor has an emitter E and two bases B1 and B2. A capacitor C charges through R from V<sub>BB</sub>. When the emitter voltage reaches the peak point V<sub>P</sub> = η V<sub>BB</sub> + V<sub>D</sub> (η is the intrinsic stand-off ratio, typically 0.5 to 0.8, and V<sub>D</sub> ≈ 0.7 V), the UJT fires and discharges C through R1, giving a sharp pulse across R1 that triggers the SCR. The period is T ≈ R C ln(1/(1 − η)).

Pulse transformer: couples the trigger pulse to the gate while isolating the control circuit from the power circuit, and can drive two SCRs from one source. Its core cannot pass a long pulse without saturating, so it carries short pulses or a pulse train.

blocks.text: R must lie between two limits for the UJT to oscillate: below (V<sub>BB</sub> − V<sub>P</sub>)/I<sub>P</sub> so that it can supply the peak-point current I<sub>P</sub>, and above (V<sub>BB</sub> − V<sub>V</sub>)/I<sub>V</sub> so that the UJT can turn off at the valley point (V<sub>V</sub>, I<sub>V</sub>).

examples.question: A 12 V trigger source drives an SCR gate. The datasheet gives V<sub>GT</sub> = 1.5 V and I<sub>GT</sub> = 100 mA. Find the series resistor R<sub>s</sub> and the peak power in it. If the gate pulse lasts 50 µs and repeats at 1 kHz, find the average power in R<sub>s</sub>.
steps: Duty ratio of the pulse: 50 µs × 1000 Hz = 0.05.
Average power: 1.05 W × 0.05 = 0.0525 W = 52.5 mW, so a 0.25 W resistor is enough for this pulse train.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 105 Ω, peak power 1.05 W, average power 52.5 mW.

examples.question: A UJT trigger circuit has V<sub>BB</sub> = 20 V, η = 0.63, V<sub>D</sub> = 0.7 V, R = 10 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF. Find the peak-point voltage and the frequency of the pulses. The UJT has I<sub>P</sub> = 10 µA, V<sub>V</sub> = 2 V and I<sub>V</sub> = 4 mA; check that R is in the working range.
steps: Check with the valley voltage (the capacitor restarts from V<sub>V</sub>, not 0): T = R C ln((V<sub>BB</sub> − V<sub>V</sub>)/(V<sub>BB</sub> − V<sub>P</sub>)) = 1 ms × ln(18 ÷ 6.7) = 0.988 ms, within 1 % of step 3.

Limits: R<sub>max</sub> = (V<sub>BB</sub> − V<sub>P</sub>)/I<sub>P</sub> = 6.7 V ÷ 10 µA = 670 kΩ; R<sub>min</sub> = (V<sub>BB</sub> − V<sub>V</sub>)/I<sub>V</sub> = 18 V ÷ 4 mA = 4.5 kΩ. 10 kΩ lies between them.
examples.answer: V<sub>P</sub> = 13.3 V and the pulses come at about 1 kHz; R = 10 kΩ is inside the 4.5 kΩ to 670 kΩ range.

traps: V<sub>GT</sub> and I<sub>GT</sub> are the values the drive must at least supply, not maximum ratings. The maximum limits are P<sub>GM</sub>, P<sub>G(AV)</sub> and the peak gate voltage and current.
R triggering cannot fire beyond 90°; RC triggering is needed for nearly 0° to 180°.
In T = R C ln(1/(1 − η)), using log base 10 gives 0.432 ms instead of 0.994 ms; the formula needs the natural log.
A pulse transformer cannot pass a long pulse: its core saturates. Use a short pulse or a pulse train.

quiz.q: List the five ways an SCR can be turned on.
quiz.a: Gate current, forward-voltage (breakover), dv/dt, temperature and light.
The gate-cathode voltage and gate current that are sure to turn on every device of the type at the stated temperature and anode voltage; the trigger circuit must supply at least these.

quiz.q: Why is the firing angle of R triggering limited to 90°?
quiz.a: The gate current comes from the supply voltage through a resistor, so it can reach I<sub>GT</sub> only while the supply is rising towards its peak; after 90° the voltage is falling, and if the threshold was not reached by the peak it will not be reached later.

quiz.q: A 15 V source triggers an SCR with V<sub>GT</sub> = 1.2 V and I<sub>GT</sub> = 50 mA. Find R<sub>s</sub> and its peak power.
An SCR in a panel false-triggers whenever a nearby contactor opens. Explain the likely cause and two fixes.
quiz.a: The contactor makes a fast voltage transient across the SCR; C<sub>j</sub> dv/dt current through J2 acts as gate current (dv/dt triggering), or noise couples into the gate leads. Fit an RC snubber across the SCR, and use a gate-cathode resistor or capacitor with short twisted gate leads.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern thyristor drives use firing ICs or microcontrollers that synchronise to the supply and give pulse trains; the UJT is now rare in new designs. Search for ‘thyristor firing circuit pulse train’ and ‘light-triggered thyristor HVDC’.
